edges.description: Mycolactone-driven tissue destruction produces the characteristic deep skin ulcer.

nodes.description: Eight weeks of rifampicin-based dual oral antibiotic therapy, combined with clarithromycin or a fluoroquinolone, is the contemporary standard treatment.

evidence.reference_title: Management of Mycobacterium ulcerans infection (Buruli ulcer) in Australia: consensus statement
evidence.snippet: There is high quality evidence to support treatment of eight weeks’ duration using rifampicin-based dual oral antibiotic therapy, in combination with clarithromycin or a fluoroquinolone

nodes.description: Mycobacterium ulcerans depends on DNA-dependent RNA polymerase for transcription. Rifampicin, the backbone of WHO-recommended antimycobacterial therapy with clarithromycin, binds the RpoB beta subunit and blocks RNA elongation; because single rpoB mutations confer high-level resistance, it is given in combination.

evidence.reference_title: Inhibition of RNA Polymerase by Rifampicin and Rifamycin-Like Molecules.
evidence.snippet: The most clinically important and extensively studied class of antibiotics known to inhibit bacterial RNAP are the rifamycins.

nodes.description: Mycolactone toxin leads to subcutaneous tissue destruction and immunosuppression, producing deep ulcers.

evidence.snippet: Mycobacterium ulcerans produces a mycolactone toxin that leads to subcutaneous tissue destruction and immunosuppression, resulting in deep ulcerations
Buruli ulcer is an indolent necrotizing disease of the skin, subcutaneous tissue, and bone
